svg.aria-label: Sequence of a regulator request: the mmci driver asks for the SD card's supply; the SCMI regulator driver sends a voltage-domain message for VOLTD_SCMI_STPMIC1_BUCK4; the arm_scmi OP-TEE transport issues an smc with the PTA-SCMI process-channel command; the OP-TEE monitor enters the secure world; OP-TEE's SCMI server looks the domain up and drives the STPMIC1 power chip over I2C4; the status returns through the monitor and the shared buffer to Linux.
svg.text: Linux wants the SD card's supply on: the trip through the secure world
On this board the secure world owns the clock tree and the power chip. Linux asks OP-TEE over SCMI, which is why the SD card works with the stock device tree.
the monitor switches to the secure world
save NS context, run the thread
smc returns to the normal world
supply on; the probe goes on
Why does a regulator need a round trip?
The power chip (STPMIC1) is on I2C4, which the kernel's tree disables: "I2C4 is managed
by OP-TEE". Every rail Linux uses is an SCMI voltage domain whose id OP-TEE maps to a
rail name in plat-stm32mp1/scmi_server.c. OP-TEE's STM32MP15 server serves voltage domains;
its STM32MP25 server does not, which is the 64-bit board's SD-card problem.
Sequence from stm32mp157f-dk2-scmi.dtsi (&sdmmc1), drivers/regulator/scmi-regulator.c, drivers/firmware/arm_scmi/transports/optee.c, core/pta/scmi.c and plat-stm32mp1/scmi_server.c.
